Density is a concentration of mass \Leftrightarrow a mass per unit volume.

With the standard symbols:

Symbol

Quantity

SI unit

\rho

Density

\mathsf{kg/m^3}

m

Mass

\mathsf{kg}

V

Volume

\mathsf{m}^3

Definition: Density

The density of a fluid is its mass per unit volume,


\displaystyle\rho = \frac{m}{V}.

It is always a good plan to stick with SI units. This makes it easier to spot mistakes and work out units you are not sure about.

Density

Calculate the density of 1.2\,\mathsf{m}^3 water with mass 1200\,\mathsf{kg}.

Solution

To find the density we need the volume of a known mass of fluid, or the mass of a known volume of fluid.

A fluid density \rho=m/V, where m is the mass and V the volume of the fluid respectively. Here, the water has mass
m=1200\,\mathsf{kg} and volume V=1.2\,\mathsf{m}^3. Hence,\rho=\frac{1200}{1.2}\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3

\implies \underline{\rho = 1000\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3}.

Symbol

Quantity

SI unit

\Rho

Relative density



\mathcal{v}

Specific volume

\mathsf{m}^3/\mathsf{kg}

Sometimes you see the density of a fluid described relative to the density of water. This is the relative density; the ratio of a fluid density to the density of water, with (\rho_w=1000\,\mathsf{kg/m}^3).

An alternative formulation you often see is the inverse of density, or specific volume. The word specific means “per unit mass”, so specific volume is the “volume per unit mass”, which is 1/\rho.

Definition: Specific volume

The specific volume of a fluid is its volume per unit mass; the inverse of its density,


\displaystyle \mathcal{v} =\frac{V}{m}= \frac{1}{\rho}.

Specific volume

A sample of water has a mass of 4.0\,\mathsf{kg} and occupies a volume of 0.0040\,\mathsf{m}^3.
Calculate the specific volume of the water.

Solution

The specific volume of the water \mathcal{v}=V/m (=1/\rho) with mass m=4.0\,\mathsf{kg} and volume V=0.0040\,\mathsf{m}^3 respectively. Hence,\mathcal{v}=\frac{0.0040}{4}\,\mathsf{m}^3/\mathsf{kg}

\implies \underline{\mathcal{v} = 0.001\,\mathsf{m}^3/\mathsf{kg}}.

Bulk density refers to the average density of an inhomogeneous substance i.e.~the total mass per unit of mixture volume.

Bulk density

A tank contains a water–solid suspension with a total mass of 120\,\mathsf{kg}. The suspension occupies 0.100\,\mathsf{m}^3.
Calculate the bulk density of the suspension.

Solution

The bulk density of the suspension \rho=m/V, where the total mass m=120\,\mathsf{kg} and total volume V=0.100\,\mathsf{m}^3. Hence,\rho=\frac{120}{0.100}\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3\implies \underline{\rho = 1200\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3}.

Fluids and especially gases comprise atoms and molecules with much space between (and within) them. We ignore these molecular level variations in mass distribution and consider most engineering fluid flows to be homogeneous.

Concept: Homogeneity

A homogeneous fluid is one for which the density is assumed to be uniform throughout the fluid, so that a single density value can be used to represent the fluid.

Your work

You can now do up to and including exercise 6 on the 

Fluid Properties chapter exercise page.

Define a fluid and its properties

Understand the key engineering assumptions for describing a fluid

Conceptualise the relationship between pressure and deformation

Evaluate pressure distributions within a static fluid

Recognise the difference between gauge and absolute pressures

Calculate fluid pressures from manometer readings

A fluid may be liquid, vapour or gas. It has no permanent shape but takes up the shape of a containing vessel or channel or is shaped by external forces (e.g.~the atmosphere).

A fluid consists of atoms/molecules in random motion
and in continual collision with the surroundings.

Fluids are readily deformable, and flow.

The key difference between liquids and gases is that where liquids have a fixed volume, gases may expand to fill container they are in.





Air expands to fill the balloon; Water is shaped first by the bottle, then by the atmosphere and finally by the glass it is poured into.

For a solid, application of a shear stress causes a deformation which, if modest (elastic), is not permanent. The solid regains original position when the stress is removed.



In a fluid under shear stress, layers of molecules slide over each other leading to continuous deformation. This occurs until the stress is removed.



Concept: Fluid deformation

A fluid is a substance for which a shear stress results in unlimited, continuous deformation.

Examples of fluid deformation

Note

Density of water \rho_w=1000\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3 (unless otherwise stated)

Gravitational acceleration g=9.81\,\mathsf{m}/\mathsf{s}^2

💧

Calculate the density of compressed air stored in a 0.1\,\mathsf{m}^3 canister with total mass total mass 25.2\,\mathsf{kg}. The canister itself has mass 26.1\,\mathsf{kg}.

✓ Check your answer

9\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3

Solution

Here, we have the mass of air m=(26.1-25.2)\,\mathsf{kg}=0.9\,\mathsf{kg} occupying V=0.1\,\mathsf{m}^3. Hence,

\displaystyle\rho=\frac{26.1-25.2}{0.1}\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3

\implies \underline{\rho = 9\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3}.

💧

A 0.005\,\mathsf{m}^3 sample of hydraulic oil has density 860\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3 at 15^\circC. Calculate the mass of the sample.

✓ Check your answer

4.3\,\mathsf{kg}

Solution

A sample with density \rho = 860\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3 and volume V=0.005\,\mathsf{m}^3 has mass m=\rho V. Hence,

m = 860\times 0.005\,\mathsf{kg}\,\mathsf{m}^3/\mathsf{m}^3


\implies \underline{m = 4.3\,\mathsf{kg}}.

💧

If 4\,\mathsf{m}^3 of oil weighs 35\,\mathsf{kN}, calculate its density and relative density.

✓ Check your answer

892\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3, \quad 0.892

Solution

Here, we have the weight of oil mg=35\times 10^3\,\mathsf{N} giving a mass m=35\times 10^3/9.81\,\mathsf{N s}^2/\mathsf{m}. This occupies a volume V=4\,\mathsf{m}^3. Hence,


\displaystyle\rho=\frac{35\times10^3}{9.81\times4}\,\mathsf{N s}^2/\mathsf{m}^4  


\implies \underline{\rho = 892\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3},
and the relative density - i.e.~the ratio of density to the density of water, is


\displaystyle\Rho = \frac{\rho}{\rho_w}=\frac{892}{1000}\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3\,\mathsf{m}^3/\mathsf{kg}

\implies \underline{\Rho = 0.892}.

💧

A compressed air system contains 0.50\,\mathsf{kg} of air. The specific volume of the air is 0.60\,\mathsf{m}^3/\mathsf{kg}. Calculate the volume occupied by the air.

✓ Check your answer

0.3\,\mathsf{m}^3

Solution

The volume of air V=\mathcal{v} m, where specific volume \mathcal{v}=0.60\,\mathsf{m}^3/\mathsf{kg} and mass m=0.50\,\mathsf{kg}. Hence,


V=0.6 \times 0.5\,\mathsf{m}^3 \mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{kg}

\implies \underline{V = 0.3\,\mathsf{m}^3}.

💧

A gas in a storage vessel occupies 15\,\mathsf{m}^3 and has a specific volume of 0.75\,\mathsf{m}^3/\mathsf{kg}. Calculate the mass of gas in the vessel.

✓ Check your answer

20\,\mathsf{kg}

Solution

The mass m of the gas with specific volume \mathcal{v} = 0.75\,\mathsf{m}^3/\mathsf{kg} and volume V=15\,\mathsf{m}^3 is m=V/\mathcal{v}. Hence,

\displaystyle m=\frac{15}{0.75}\,\mathsf{m}^3 \mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3

\implies \underline{m = 20\,\mathsf{kg}}.

💧

An air–water droplet spray has a bulk density of 25\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3. A spray cloud occupies a volume of 0.40\,\mathsf{m}^3.
Calculate the total mass of liquid and air contained within the spray cloud.

✓ Check your answer

10\,\mathsf{kg}

Solution

The bulk density of the spray \rho=m/V = 25\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3 with volume V=0.40\,\mathsf{m}^3. Hence, the total mass of liquid and air m = \rho V with

m= 25 \times 0.40\,\mathsf{kg} \mathsf{m}^3/\mathsf{m}^3  

\implies \underline{m = 10\,\mathsf{kg}}.

📝

A piston-cylinder device contains air at an absolute pressure of 250\,\mathrm{kPa} and a temperature of 20^\circ\mathrm{C}. The air occupies a volume of 0.080\,\mathrm{m^3}.

The piston is allowed to move freely, and the air expands until its pressure is reduced to 150\,\mathrm{kPa}. During the expansion, the air cools to a temperature of 5^\circ\mathrm{C}.

Assuming that the air behaves as a perfect gas, determine the final volume of the air in \mathrm{m^3}.

✓ Check your answer

0.126\,\mathrm{m^3}

Solution

For a fixed mass of perfect gas,

\displaystyle \frac{p_1V_1}{T_1}=\frac{p_2V_2}{T_2},

which rearranges for final volume

\displaystyle V_2=\frac{p_1V_1T_2}{p_2T_1}.

Converting temperatures to Kelvin,


T_1 = 20+273.15 = 293.15\,\mathrm{K} \quad\mathrm{and}\quad T_2 = 5+273.15 = 278.15\,\mathrm{K},

we can substitute values


\displaystyle V_2=\frac{(250\times10^3\times 0.080\times278.15}{150\times10^3\times 293.15}.


\implies \underline{V_2 = 0.126\,\mathrm{m^3}}

The air therefore expands from 0.080\,\mathrm{m^3} to approximately 0.126\,\mathrm{m^3}.

💧

Find the pressure relative to atmospheric pressure experienced by a diver working on the sea bed at a depth of 35\,\mathsf{m}. Take the density of sea water to be 1030\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3.

✓ Check your answer

353.7\,\mathsf{kPa}\approx 3.54\,\mathsf{bar}

Solution

The pressure relative to atmospheric pressure is the gauge pressure due to the liquid above the diver,


p=\rho g h

where \rho=1030\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3, g=9.81\,\mathsf{m}/\mathsf{s}^2 and h=35\,\mathsf{m}. Hence,


p=1030\times9.81\times35\,\mathsf{Pa}


\implies \underline{p=353.7\,\mathsf{kPa}\approx3.54\,\mathsf{bar}}.

Hint

To check think through your units, with pressure p=F/A \implies \mathsf{N}/\mathsf{m}^2, force F=ma \implies \mathsf{kg}\,\mathsf{m}/\mathsf{s}^2 or \mathsf{N}. Therefore pressure has units \mathsf{kg}\,\mathsf{m}/\mathsf{s}^2\mathsf{m}^2, simplifying to \mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}\,\mathsf{s}^2 which is Pascals \mathsf{Pa}.

💧

An open glass is sitting on a table. It has a diameter of 10\,\mathsf{cm}. If water up to a height of 20\,\mathsf{cm} is now added, calculate the force exerted onto the table by the addition of the water.

✓ Check your answer

15.41\,\mathsf{N}

Solution

You can ignore both the weight of the glass and atmospheric pressure since they were there originally and you are only interested in the extra force exerted onto the table due to the addition of the water.

The force exerted on the table by the water is equal to the weight dues to the hydrostatic pressure acting on the base of the glass, p=\rho g h.

Force F=pA, where A is the surface area of the glass base.

Hence,

\displaystyle F=\rho g h \pi r^2 = 1000\times9.81\times\frac{20}{100}\pi\left(\frac{10}{2\times 100}\right)^2\,\frac{\mathsf{kg\,m\,m}\,\mathsf{m}^2}{\mathsf{m}^3\mathsf{s}^2}

 \implies \underline{F=15.41\,\mathsf{N}}

📝

A closed rectangular tank with internal dimensions 6\,\mathsf{m}\times3\,\mathsf{m}\times1.5\,\mathsf{m} high has a vertical riser pipe of cross-sectional area 0.001\,\mathsf{m}^2 in the upper surface, as shown in Figure Q10. The tank and riser are filled with water such that the water level in the riser pipe is 3.5,\mathsf{m} above the top of the tank. Atmospheric pressure is 1\,\mathsf{bar}.



Figure Q10: Sketch of tank with riser (not to scale)

Calculate

The gauge pressure at the top of the tank.

The gauge pressure at the base of the tank.

The force exerted on the base of the tank due to the gauge water pressure.

The weight of water in the tank and riser.

Explain the difference between (3) and (4).

Hint

It may be helpful to think about the force on the top of the tank.

✓ Check your answer

34.3\,\mathsf{kPa}

49.05\,\mathsf{kPa}

882.9\,\mathsf{kN}

264.9\,\mathsf{kN}

Solution

The water level in the riser is 3.5\,\mathsf{m} above the top of the tank. Therefore, the pressure at the top of the tank is determined by a water column of height 3.5\,\mathsf{m}.

The gauge pressure at the top

 p_{\mathrm{top}}=3.5 \rho_w g ,  \implies \underline{p_{\mathrm{top}}=34.3\,\mathsf{kPa}} .

The total depth from the water surface in the riser to the base of the tank

 h=3.5+1.5=5.0\,\mathsf{m}.

Hence, the gauge pressure at the base

 p_{\mathrm{base}}=5.0 \rho_w g ,   \implies \underline{p_{\mathrm{base}}=49.05\,\mathsf{kPa}} 

The area of the base of the tank

 A=6\times3=18\,\mathsf{m}^2.

Therefore, the force exerted on the base due to the gauge pressure

 F_{\mathrm{base}}=p_{\mathrm{base}}A

 =49.05\times10^3\times18\,\mathsf{N},  \implies \underline{F_{\mathrm{base}}=882.9\,\mathsf{kN}}

The volume of water in the rectangular tank

 V_{\mathrm{tank}}=6\times3\times1.5=27\,\mathsf{m}^3 

and the volume of water in the riser

 V_{\mathrm{riser}}=0.001\times3.5=0.0035\,\mathsf{m}^3.

Thus,

 V_{\mathrm{total}}=27.0035\,\mathsf{m}^3 

and the weight of water

 W=\rho_w V_{\mathrm{total}}g ,  \implies \underline{W=264.9\,\mathsf{kN}} .

The force on the base is therefore much greater than the weight of water. This is because the pressure at the top surface of the tank is also above atmospheric pressure, producing an upward force on the top of the tank. The difference between the downward force on the base and the upward force on the top is the weight of the water.

📝

A double U-tube manometer is connected to a pipe as shown in Figure Q11. Taking the dimensions and fluids as indicated, calculate the absolute pressure at point A (centre of the pipe).

Take atmospheric pressure as 1.01\,\mathsf{bar} and the density of mercury as 13600\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3.



Figure Q11: Double U-tube manometer with readings, for use with exercise 11 (not to scale)

✓ Check your answer

124.7\,\mathsf{kPa}

Solution

We start the analysis from the point where we know what the condition is, in this case atmospheric pressure on the far right of the system. We then chose horizontal planes within the same fluid where there is an interface, this is because we know that the pressure is constant since pressure is constant at any horizontal plane in the same fluid. We chose interface points as this allows us to define each point in the system as a function of the known pressure, atmospheric pressure on the far right.



Figure Q11s: Double U-tube manometer showing equilibrium level choices for solution (not to scale)

In the far right hand arm at level 1

p_1=p_{\mathrm{atm}}

and at level 2

p_2=p_1+\rho_wgh_1 = p_{\mathrm{atm}}+\rho_wgh_1 \quad\dots(\ast).

In the second limb from right, level 2 also exists within the water layer and p_2'=p_2. In the  second and third limbs from the right, level 2 exists in air and in both. Hence p_2''=p_2'=p_2.

Level 3 connects the mercury in the third from right limb to the left hand limb with

p_3=p_2''+\rho_mgh_2 and

p_3'=p_A+\rho_wgh_3. With p_3=p_3'

p_A=p_2''+\rho_mgh_2 - \rho_wgh_3 = p_2+\rho_mgh_2 - \rho_wgh_3.

Eliminating p_2 from (\ast)

p_A = p_{\mathrm{atm}}+ g(\rho_wh_1 +\rho_mh_2 - \rho_wh_3)

With

 p_{\mathrm{atm}}=1.01\times10^5\,\mathsf{Pa}, \qquad \rho_{\mathrm{Hg}}=13600\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3 

Hence,

 \underline{p_A=124.7\,\mathsf{kPa}} 

📝

An inverted U-tube manometer connects pipes A and B as shown in Figure Q12. The manometer fluid is oil of density 900\,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3; pipes A and B contain water.



Figure Q12: Inverted U-tube manometer with readings, for use with exercise 12 (not to scale)

Calculate p_A-p_B, where p_A and p_B are the pressures at the pipe centres, as shown.

Hint

Think about what you are required to calculate. Can you calculate directly?

✓ Check your answer

-4.218\,\mathsf{kPa}

Solution

The key to this question is to realise that you are calculating the difference between pressures at A and B.

So we chose points in the system that allow us to understand/relate the pressures at A and B. We know that the pressure within the same fluid is constant at the same horizontal plane. So we analyse first the left hand arm, and then the right hand arm at the level of the top manometer fluid interface.

We need the difference between the pressures at A and B, so there is no need to calculate either pressure individually.



Figure Q12s: Inverted U-tube manometer showing equilibrium level choices for solution (not to scale)

In the left hand limb

p_1 = p_A - \rho_w g h_1. \quad\dots(\ast)

In the right hand limb, the pressure at that level p_1'=p_1, by equilibrium. But we can also write this pressure in terms of p_B,

p_B = p_1 + \rho_ogh_2 + \rho_wgh_3.

Eliminating p_1 using (\ast)

p_B = p_A - \rho_w g h_1 + \rho_ogh_2 + \rho_wgh_3 and

p_A-p_B = \rho_w g h_1 - \rho_ogh_2 - \rho_wgh_3

Using \rho_w=1000,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3 and \rho_{\mathrm{oil}}=900,\mathsf{kg}/\mathsf{m}^3, with h_1=0.45\,\mathsf{m}, h_2=0.2\,\mathsf{m} and h_3=0.7\,\mathsf{m},

 \underline{p_A-p_B=-4.218\,\mathsf{kPa}}.

📝

Figure Q13 shows two enclosed tanks, A and B, which are partially filled with a liquid of relative density 0.82.  The free surface in tank A is 2\,\mathsf{m} below that in tank B. The pressures at the corresponding free surfaces are p_A and p_B with p_A > p_B.  The tanks are connected to a u-tube manometer containing mercury of relative density 13.56 (density relative to water).



Figure Q13: Enclosed tanks connected by a manometer with readings, for use with exercise 13 (not to scale)

Determine the pressure difference p_A - p_B when the difference in mercury levels is 225\,\mathsf{mm}.

✓ Check your answer

44.209\,\mathsf{kPa}

Solution

The trick here is to realise that you can analyse the left hand and right hand arms of the system, allowing you to directly relate the difference between the pressures p_A and p_B.



Figure Q13s: Enclosed tanks connected by a manometer with readings

p_x = p_A+\rho_1gz_1 = p_B+(z_2+2)\rho_1g+0.225\rho_mg

Rearranging for the pressure difference

p_A-p_B = 0.225\rho_mg+(z_2-z_1+2)\rho_1g)

\quad = g[0.225\rho_m+(2-0.225)\rho_1].

But we know \rho_m and \rho_1 as their relative densities, hence

p_A-p_B = \rho_wg[0.225\Rho_m + 1.775\Rho_1] = 1000\times 9.81[0.225\times 13.6 + 1.775\times 0.82] 

\implies \underline{p_A-p_B=44.209\,\mathsf{kPa}}

I would encourage you to annotate as we go through - to pick out e.g.~key words, things you find challenging, or helpful alternative explanations. Exercise sheet questions are grouped in 3 categories.

📝 Exam style questions using those techniques. You may need to make decisions about the appropriate techniques are to use, work to navigate your way through setting up the problem, or interpret the results.

Here we consider how the principles of hydrostatic pressure can be used in devices to measure pressure.

A piezometer is a simple device for measuring moderate pressures - or differences in pressure - in a liquid (but not a gas).



The diagram above shows a pipeline containing liquid of density \rho. A piezometer is mounted to measure the pressure at point A. This consists of a thin, vertical, transparent tube with one end inserted into the top of the pipeline via a tapping, with the other end open to the atmosphere.

The elevated pressure in the pipeline liquid causes that liquid to rise up the piezometer tube to form a static column with height h_A. The free surface of this liquid column is at atmospheric pressure.

Therefore, at the base of the liquid column the gauge pressure must be p_A=\rho gh_A.

Similarly, if a second piezometer tube is placed at tapping B, pressure in the liquid at B causes a static column of pipeline liquid with height h_B to form. The gauge pressure p_B at point B is p_B=\rho gh_B.

Together, the two piezometers measure the pressure difference p_A-p_B between the two points


p_A-p_B=\rho gh_A-\rho gh_B = \rho g(h_A-h_B).

The pressure difference is determined by measuring the difference in height between the two liquid columns (h_A-h_B), given the known pipeline fluid density \rho.

Notes on piezometers

The measured pressures are gauge pressures. Because the piezometer is open to the atmosphere, the hydrostatic pressure due to the static column height will be relative to atmospheric.

A piezometer is open to the atmosphere and so is only suitable to measure pressures in liquids and not gasses. A gas would simply escape.

A manometer shares the underlying principle of the piezometer, with the addition of a second liquid between the pipeline fluid and the atmospheric free surface. This means that a manometer can measure pressures in any fluid - liquid or gas.



The intermediary fluid is termed the “working liquid” or “manometric liquid”, with density \rho_m. In the configuration shown, with the working liquid sitting below the pipeline liquid, \rho_m>\rho; the two are immiscible, such that an interface forms between them.

The pressure in the pipeline forces some of the fluid into the manometer tube, pushing the working fluid, such that the positions of the interfaces in each limb of the manometer shift. The pressure p_A at point A is directly related to this shift in interface levels; to be found by balancing the hydrostatic contributions of the different fluids in the manometer.

Drawing an imaginary horizontal line (X in the diagram) through the lower interface, we note that the pressure in the left-hand limb at this level must be the same as the pressure in the right-hand limb. This must be true for the manometer to be in equilibrium - i.e. with no flow.

From the left-hand limb, the pressure at the interface


p_X=p_A+\rho gh_1.

Similarly in the right-hand limb

p_X=\rho_mgh_2.

Equating eliminates p_X and


p_A=g(\rho_mh_2-\rho h_1).

Hence the pressure p_A can be determined by measuring the two heights h_1 and h_2, for the known fluid densities \rho and \rho_m.

For example, if the pipeline above contains air with density \rho=1.2\,kg/m^3 and the working fluid is water with density \rho_m=1000\,kg/m^3, with the heights measured h_1=0.3\,m and h_2=0.1\,m, we can evaluate the gauge pressure in the air


p_A=g(\rho_mh_2-\rho h_1)=9.81(1000\times0.1-1.2\times0.3)\,Pa


\implies \underline {p_A=977\,\text{Pa}}.

Notes on manometers

The pressures above are all gauge pressures. The tube is open to the atmosphere which creates the reference pressure.

If the pipeline fluid is gas, the manometric liquid is typically water \rho_m=\rho_{H_2O}=1000\,kg/m^3 or some form of oil \rho_m\approx 800 to 900\,kg/m^3.

If the pipeline contains a flowing liquid, the manometric liquid is typically mercury \rho_m=\rho_{Hg}=13600\,kg/m^3.

If we have no reference pressure, we can still evaluate pressure differences using this method using a differential manometer (see worked example).

Evaluating pressures from a manometer

Pressures are constant in a horizontal plane: identify the plane that exists in two arms of the manometer.

Construct the hydrostatic balances in each limb, recalling that the 

hydrostatic pressure at the base of a water column is that at the top of the column, plus the hydrostatic contribution \rho g h of the column.

Apply equilibrium by equating the pressures in the two limbs at the identified plane.

Differential manometer

Two pipelines convey a gas with density \rho. A differential manometer with a working fluid of density \rho_m measures the pressure difference p_A-p_B, between point A and point B in the respective pipelines.



The pressure difference can be found by measuring the heights h_1 and h_2. Show that


p_A-p_B=(\rho_m-\rho)(h_1-h_2)g,

and hence find the pressure difference when \rho=1.2\,kg/m^3, \rho_m=800\,kg/m^3, h_1=58\,mm and h_2=176\,mm.

Solution

We note that the horizontal plane X intersects each limb of the manometer and exists within one fluid; applying equilibrium at X in each limb will relate p_A and p_B.

In the left-hand limb


p_X=p_A+\rho gh_1 + \rho_m g(h_2-h_1),

and in the right-hand limb


p_X=p_B+\rho g h_2.

Equating eliminates p_X, with


p_A-p_B= \rho g h_2 - \rho gh_1 - \rho_m g(h_2-h_1).

Collecting terms in \rho and \rho_m, we can rearrange


p_A-p_B= \rho g(h_2-h_1) - \rho_m g(h_2-h_1) = g(\rho -\rho_m)(h_2-h_1)

or


\underline{p_A-p_B= g(\rho_m -\rho)(h_1-h_2)}

as required.

Evaluating

Evaluating from the data provided


p_A-p_B= g(\rho_m -\rho)(h_1-h_2) = 9.81\times(800-1.2)(58-176)\times 10^{-3},Pa,


\implies \underline{p_A-p_B=-925\,\mathsf{kPa}.}

🔥 Challenge manometer example

A manometer consists of two tubes A and B, with vertical axes and uniform cross-sectional areas A_a=500\,mm^2 and A_b=800\,mm^2 respectively, connected by a U-tube C of cross-sectional area A_c=70\,mm^2 throughout - shown in the figure below.  Tube A contains a liquid of relative density \Rho_a=0.8, tube B contains one of relative density \Rho_b=0.9.  The surface of separation between the two liquids is in the vertical side of C connected to tube A.  Determine the additional pressure, \Delta p_B that, when applied to tube B, will cause the surface of separation to rise \Delta h_c=60\,mm in tube C.



Solution

The surface in tube B moves down a distance \Delta h_b due to the additional pressure applied, and liquid B is pushed into tube C. The interface between the two fluids in the left hand manometer arm (“the surface of separation”) is pushed upwards due to this additional fluid.

The rise in the surface of separation will push liquid A up into tube A, raising the surface in tube A a distance \Delta h_a - shown in the diagram below.



The volume change in tubes A, B and C must match each other. We can express this mathematically in terms of the height changes and the constant cross_sectional areas


A_c\Delta h_c = A_b\Delta h_b = A_a\Delta h_a.

From here, we can find the changes in depth in each tube


\displaystyle \Delta h_a = \frac{A_c\Delta h_c}{A_a}, \quad \text{and} \quad \Delta h_b = \frac{A_c\Delta h_c}{A_b}.

Before the extra pressure was added in tube B, the manometer was in equilibrium with the fluid depths in tubes A and B h_a and h_b respectively. In the left-hand arm at level 1 (horizontal plane of constant pressure existing in both arms) in the diagram


p_1=p_A+\rho_a gh_a

and in the right-hand arm


p_1=p_B+\rho_b gh_b.

Equibibrium in the manometer after the pressure is added is given at level 2 in the diagram. In the left-hand arm


p_2=p_A+\rho_a g(h_a+\Delta h_a - \Delta h_c),

and in the right-hand arm


p_2=p_B+\Delta p_B + \rho_b g(h_b-\Delta h_b - \Delta h_c).

Subracting the before from the after scenario in each arm can give us a pair of equations for p_2-p_1.

In the left-hand arm


p_2-p_1 = p_A+\rho_a g(h_a+\Delta h_a - \Delta h_c) - p_A -\rho_a gh_a,

which simplifies to

p_2-p_1=\rho_a g(\Delta h_a - \Delta h_c).

Similarly in the right-hand arm


p_2-p_1 = p_B+\Delta p_B + \rho_b g(h_b-\Delta h_b - \Delta h_c) - p_B - \rho_b gh_b,

simplifying to


p_2-p_1 = \Delta p_B - \rho_b g(\Delta h_b + \Delta h_c).

Equating p_2-p_1 from the left and right-hand arms


\rho_a g(\Delta h_a - \Delta h_c)= \Delta p_B - \rho_b g(\Delta h_b + \Delta h_c),

which can be rewritten for the pressure change we are looking for


\Delta p_B = \rho_a g(\Delta h_a - \Delta h_c) + \rho_b g(\Delta h_b + \Delta h_c).

From our first step, we related the changes in depth in each tube, so we can write \Delta p_B now in terms of data provided


\displaystyle \Delta p_B = g\rho_w\left\{\Rho_a\left[\Delta h_c\left( \frac{A_c}{A_a} - 1\right)\right] + \Rho_b\left[\Delta h_c\left( \frac{A_c}{A_b} + 1\right)\right]\right\}.

Evaluating from the data provided


\displaystyle \Delta p_B = 9.81\times1000\left\{0.8\left[\frac{60}{1000}\left( \frac{70}{500} - 1\right)\right] + 0.9\left[\frac{60}{1000}\left( \frac{70}{800} + 1\right)\right]\right\}\,\mathsf{Pa},


\implies \underline{\Delta p_B = 172\,\mathsf{Pa}}.

In a fluid (liquid or gas) molecules are in continuous motion \rightarrow There is an amount of energy associated with this motion.



When the molecules interact with each other there is an equal and opposite reaction - therefore no net force. But when the molecules interact with walls, there is a resultant force perpendicular to the surface. Each impact force is tiny, but there are many of them.





If we consider a tiny element of wall area \delta A, we can imagine a single molecule exerting a force \delta F on that. The pressure exerted on the wall by the molecule is defined as the force per unit area, or

\displaystyle p=\frac{\delta F}{\delta A}.



To find the total force, and hence pressure, we need to sum up all the molecular-level contributions over the full surface, i.e.~F = \sum \delta F.

In the limit \delta A,\,\,\delta F \rightarrow 0, F \rightarrow \int\,dF, and

F=\int p\,dA.

In the case of constant pressure, we can integrate with

\displaystyle F = \frac{p}{A}\quad, \quad p=\frac{F}{A}.

These definitions hold if the pressure is constant or an average value is appropriate. In many instances this is not the case - to be discussed!

Definition: Pressure

Pressure is an energy density within a fluid, characterised by molecular-level motion. This equates to the force (F) exerted by a fluid per unit area (A) of surface to which it is applied.


\displaystyle p=\frac{F}{A}.

Notes about pressure

Pressure is a scalar quantity, acting equally in all directions. Compared to a force, which is a vector with magnitude and direction.

Pressure has the units of force per unit area, which is a stress.

Gases cannot sustain tensile stress, liquids a negligible amount.

The force exerted on a vessel by fluid pressure acts perpendicular (normal) to the vessel surface.

The vessel walls exert an equal and opposite force on the fluid.

Molecular fluctuations are also responsible for heat (as indicated by temperature), meaning there is a relationship between the pressure and temperature of a fluid. Hence why you study fluid mechanics and thermodynamics in the same module!

Concept: A Perfect Gas

In a Perfect Gas the molecules behave as perfectly elastic small spheres, influencing each other only when they collide and so smalle that they occupy a tiny proportion of the volume of space in which they move.

No real gas is a perfect gas, though many behave nearly so. Luckily, air is close to a perfect gas.

In a perfect gas, there is a direct relationship between pressure and temperature.

A common unit of pressure (not SI) is \mathsf{bar}, where 1\,\mathsf{bar}=10^5\mathsf{Pa}. This is convenient, because 1\,\mathsf{bar} is close to atmospheric pressure.

Definition: The Perfect Gas Law

The product of the pressure and volume of a perfect gas is directly proportional to the product of its absolute temperature and amount of substance, with a universal constant of proportionality R - the Universal Gas Constant. Hence,


\displaystyle pV=nRT \quad\mathrm{or}\quad p=\rho RT,

where R=8.31445\,\mathsf{J/mol\,K}.

Perfect gas law

A hydrogen balloon is to expand to a sphere of 20\,\mathsf{m} diameter at a height of 30\,\mathsf{km} where the air pressure is 1100\,\mathsf{Pa} and the temperature is -40^\circ\mathsf{C}. If there is to be no stress in the fabric of the balloon (i.e.~the pressure inside the balloon equals the pressure outside), what volume of hydrogen must be added at ground level where the air pressure is 101.3\,\mathsf{kPa} and the temperature is 15^\circ\mathsf{C}?

Solution

So we have 2 different states we need to look at; at ground level (1) and at 30\,\mathsf{km} (2). We know the temperature and pressure at each state and we know that the hydrogen obeys the Perfect Gas law. The conditions at the two elevations give us the proportionality in the law, which relates to the amount of gas and therfore the volume we are asked for.

At ground level p_1V_1=nRT_1, and at 30\,\mathsf{km} p_2V_2=nRT_2. Hence, nR remains constant over the ascent and

\displaystyle \frac{p_1V_1}{T_1}=\frac{p_2V_2}{T_2}. Rearranging for the (required) volume at ground level V_1

\displaystyle V_1=\frac{p_2V_2T_1}{p_1T_2}

At 30\,\mathsf{km} the balloon is a sphere with diameter 20\,\mathsf{m} with volume

\displaystyle V_2=\frac{4}{3}\pi\left(\frac{20}{2}\right)^3.

Using the data in the question, with temperatures as absolute temperatures in Kelvin

\displaystyle V_1=\frac{4}{3}\pi\left(\frac{20}{2}\right)^3 \frac{1100(273+15)}{101.3\times10^3(273-40)}\,\mathsf{m}^3\frac{\mathsf{Pa\,K}}{\mathsf{Pa\,K}}

\implies \underline{V_1=56.2\,\mathsf{m}^3}

Note that the volume at altitude V_2\approx 4200\,\mathsf{m}^3 - the gas has expanded around 75 times its original volume!

Concept: Thought experiment

Straw with fluid

What happens to the pressure in a straw when you place your finger over the top and try to pull the straw out of a glass of water?

What forces are acting, and why doesn’t the water simply fall out?

See explanation

The water is held in the straw because the pressure above the water is lower than the atmospheric pressure acting at the bottom of the water column.

Why is the pressure above the column lower than atmospheric pressure?

Take a look at the Perfect Gas Law. We have a fixed amount of air trapped between the water column and your finger. If the temperature is constant, the Perfect Gas Law tells us that


pV=nRT=\text{constant}.

Therefore, an increase in the volume of the trapped air must be accompanied by a decrease in its pressure.

When you first start to lift the straw, some of the water flows out of the bottom of the straw. This increases the volume of air trapped above the water column, causing its pressure to decrease. The volume increases until the pressure difference between the atmospheric pressure at the bottom of the column and the reduced pressure at the top is sufficient to support the weight of the water column.

The resulting force balance (for a straw with cross-sectional area A) is


(p_\mathrm{atm}-p_\mathrm{top})A=\rho ghA,

giving


p_\mathrm{atm}-p_\mathrm{top}=\rho gh.

So the pressure difference is exactly what is required to support the weight of the water column.

You can see from the Perfect Gas Law that pressure is not just linked to temperature, but also to density. The relationship between pressure and density depends on the compressibility of the fluid. For low to intermediate flow speeds, much less than the speed of sound in the fluid, we can usually assume that flows are incompressible, and the density is the same everywhere. We will explore compressible flows later in the course.

Concept: Compressibility

An incompressible fluid is one for which changes in pressure cause negligible changes in density.

Furthermore, we typically assume that the rapid molecular-level fluctuations that give rise to the pressure and temperature in a fluid can be time-averaged by treating the fluid as a continuum.

Concept: Continuum assumption

The continuum assumption treats a fluid as a continuous medium, so that fluid properties such as pressure, temperature and density can be described by smoothly varying, time-averaged quantities rather than by the motion of individual molecules.

In a liquid the molecules are bound to each other by forces of molecular attraction (cohesion). At a boundary between two fluids this gives rise to “surface tension”.

Symbol

Surface tension



\mathsf{N/m}







Examples of surface tension: A fluid jet breaking up into droplets; A water-boatman using surface tension to support it’s weight; Oil will not mix with water.

Surface tension can also affect pressure. Although surface tension is introduced as an interfacial energy, it also represents a force acting along the interface. When the interface is curved, these surface-tension forces have a resultant normal to the interface. This must be balanced by a pressure difference across the interface.

For an interface with principal radii of curvature R_1 and R_2, the pressure jump is given by the Young-Laplace equation

 \Delta p = \gamma \left( \frac{1}{R_1}+\frac{1}{R_2} \right). 

Notice that a flat interface has zero curvature, so surface tension does not produce a pressure difference across it. A curved interface, such as the surface of a droplet or bubble, does.

Pressure inside a water droplet

A spherical water droplet has a radius of 1,\mathsf{mm}. The surface tension of water is \gamma=0.072\,\mathsf{N/m}. If the pressure outside the droplet is atmospheric, p_\mathrm{atm}=101.3\,\mathsf{kPa}, determine the pressure inside the droplet.

Solution

For a spherical interface, the Young-Laplace equation gives the difference in pressures inside and outside the droplet


\displaystyle \Delta p=\frac{2\gamma}{R} = \frac{2\times 0.072}{1\times10^{-3}}=144\,\mathsf{Pa}.

Therefore the pressure inside the droplet its this pressure difference above atmospheric pressure


p_{\mathrm{drop}}=p_\mathrm{atm}+\Delta p = 101.3+0.144\,\mathsf{kPa}


\implies \underline{p_{\mathrm{drop}}=101.444\,\mathsf{kPa}}.

The pressure inside the droplet is therefore slightly higher than the pressure outside because the surface tension of the curved interface must be balanced by a pressure difference.

Because pressure fundamentally arises from molecular motion, zero pressure occurs when that motion ceases. That is, at absolute zero, zero Kelvin; a vacuum.

However, in engineering we usually deal with differences in pressure where the system is subject to the atmosphere. It is usually convenient to “zero” pressure measurements relative to atomspheric pressure.

Definition: Absolute and gauge pressures

Absolute pressure is fluid pressure relative to zero pressure, a vacuum.

Gauge pressure is the fluid pressure relative to atmospheric pressure.

Hence, gauge pressure = absolute pressure - atmospheric pressure

Gauge pressure is typically used in industry. If absolute pressure is 3\,\mathsf{bar} and atmospheric pressure is 1\,\mathsf{bar}, then gauge pressure will be 2\,\mathsf{bar}.

Note that atmospheric pressure changes with altitude, temperature, weather!

Fluid at rest has constant pressure across a horizontal plane - this is why liquid surfaces are flat and horizontal. But there is a pressure gradient in the vertical direction. So how does pressure vary with depth in a fluid?

Concept: Thought experiment

If the bottle in the picture is filled with water so that a jet squirts out of each hole, which of the thress jets travels furthest?



See explanation



Water is pushed out of the hole by the weight of the fluid sitting above it. The bottom hole has the deepest column of fluid above it, so the jet here will have the highest velocity. The bottome jet will travel further than the jets from the holes higher up on the bottle.

It is the vertical gradient of hydrostatic pressure in the fluid that drives the jet out of the bottle.

Consider a small element of stationary fluid. The fluid is at rest, so there are no shear forces acting on the element, and the horizontal pressure is constant. However, the element has weight, \delta m g, acting vertically downwards. Because the element is stationary it must be in equilibrium \rightarrow the sum of all the forces acting on the element must be zero, \sum \text{Forces} = 0.

The weight of the fluid element is counteracted by the difference in pressures acting vertically on the bottom and top surfaces of the element, as shown in the schematic.



Considering the forces in the vertical, z, direction, we have

weight \delta m g acting downwards,

a force due to the pressure acting upwards on the bottom surface of the element due to the water below it, F_z = p \delta x \delta y,

a force due to the pressure acting downwards on the top surface of the element due to the water above it, F_z +\delta F_z = (p + \delta p) \delta x \delta y.



Resolving these vertical forces to ensure equilibrium, their sum must be zero with


F_z-(F_z+\delta F_z) - \delta mg = 0.

In terms of the element properties, from above


p \delta x \delta y - (p + \delta p) \delta x \delta y - g(\rho\delta x \delta y\delta z)=0.

This simplifies to


\delta p \delta x \delta y = - g(\rho\delta x \delta y\delta z),

and so


\displaystyle \frac{\delta p}{\delta z} = - \rho g.

And so, in the limit as \delta z \rightarrow 0, the element becomes infinitessimally small and we form the differential eqution describing the vertical, hydrostatic pressure distribution in a stationary fluid


\displaystyle \frac{dp}{dz} = - \rho g.

For a homogeneous and incompressible fluid, density is assumed constant, and we can integrate to find the pressure difference between point 1 and point 2 in a fluid


\displaystyle \int_1^2\,dp = -\rho g\int_1^2\,dz \qquad \implies \qquad p_2-p_1 = -\rho g(z_2-z_1)

or


\Delta p = -\rho g\Delta z.

Take care of your coordinates

Note that here we have defined the vertical coordinate z as positive upwards i.e. gravity and hence weight are negative quantities and hydrostatic pressure decreases with increasing z. Often you will see depth or elevation defined in the downwards direction, in the same direction as gravity. Clearly in that case, hydrostatic pressure increases with increasing depth h following


\Delta p = \rho g\Delta h.

Essentially, it does not matter how you define these so long as you are consistent. Always define your coordinates before working on a problem and stick to your definition.

Definition: Hydrostatic pressure

Hydrostatic pressure is the pressure within a fluid that is at rest, resulting from the weight of the fluid above the point of interest. Hence,


\displaystyle p=p_0 + \rho g h.

where p_0 is the pressure at the reference surface and h is the vertical depth below that surface.

Hydrostatic pressure

Atmospheric pressure of 1.01\,\mathsf{bar} acts on the surface of a lake 10\,\mathsf{m} deep. Find the absolute pressure at the bottom of the lake.

Solution

If we denote the top of the lake to be at elevation z_1 and pressure p_1=p_{\mathrm{atm}}, and the bottom of the lake with elevation z_2 and pressure p_2, then the pressure at the bottom of the lake is due to the atmospheric pressure acting on the surface plus the hydrostatic pressure of the fluid above the base


p_2 = p_{\mathrm{atm}} + \rho_wg(z_1-z_2).

The difference in elevations z_1-z_2=10\,\mathsf{m}, hence


p_2 = 1.01\times 10^5 + 1000 \times 9.81 \times 10\,\mathsf{Pa}.


\implies \underline {p_2 = 199100\,\mathsf{Pa} =  199.1\,\mathsf{kPa} =  1.991\,\mathsf{bar}}.
